entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The College of Cardinals, established in the 11th century, is an assembly of senior ecclesiastical leaders within the Catholic Church, primarily responsible for electing the Pope. With its origins in the early Christian community of Rome, the College has evolved into a vital institution that influences not only the governance of the Church but also the socio-political landscape of Southern Europe and beyond. Noteworthy figures such as Cardinal Richelieu of France and Cardinal Wolsey of England illustrate the intersection of religious authority and political power, shaping decisions that have reverberated through history.

Throughout its history, the College of Cardinals has played a pivotal role in significant events such as the papal elections, notably the conclave of 1268-1271 that lasted nearly three years, showcasing the complexities of Church politics. The Cardinals often acted as advisors to the Pope and, at times, wielded substantial power in their own right, as seen during the Avignon Papacy (1309-1377), when the papacy was heavily influenced by the French monarchy. This period saw the Cardinals navigating the delicate balance between spiritual leadership and temporal authority, further cementing their importance within the fabric of European politics.

The legacy of the College of Cardinals extends into the modern era, where it continues to influence the Catholic Church's stance on global issues, from social justice to interfaith dialogue. The composition of the College has transformed over the centuries, reflecting the Church's response to broader societal changes, including the rise of global Catholicism in the Global South. As Pope Francis stated, 'The Church is called to be a sign of hope,' highlighting the ongoing relevance of the Cardinals in guiding the Church through contemporary challenges.
